messages.author: f2b64d27814968e8
messages.subject: Variance of n
parts:
I've been trying for 2 days now to finalize an abundance estimate for
whales. The final estimator is much like that in the example given in 8.5
of the textbook. There is stratification over blocks and two categories of
Beaufort sea state. Hence the final estimates of abundance and variance
must be worked out outside of the Distance program, as it cannot handle two
levels of stratification.

My problem has been the calculation of the variance of the total population
estimate, N. I have followed closely the example given on p. 388-390 of the
text, but have not been able to derive an answer that seems reasonable. I
suspect I am doing something very basically wrong, and my prime suspect is
my calculation of var(n), where n is the number of sightings. This is
required for the calculation.

On a basic level, I do not actually understand how n can have a variance,
since it is not estimated. However n/L (encounter rate) does certainly have
a variance. My assumption has been that var(n) can be calculated by scaling
the SE of n/L by L, then squaring. But perhaps I am wrong about this?

I am sorry if this seems a trivial question.

Best regards,

Daniel Pike

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Variance of n
parts:
> > On a basic level, I do not actually understand how n can have a variance,
> > since it is not estimated. However n/L (encounter rate) does certainly have
> > a variance. My assumption has been that var(n) can be calculated by scaling
> > the SE of n/L by L, then squaring. But perhaps I am wrong about this?

Daniel, the material you need is on p90 of the book. Note that you need a
weighted sample variance of encounter rate, weighted by line length. As n
is just a constant (L) times the encounter rate, clearly it can have a
variance. It is an estimator of the expected sample size, E(n) (see for
example p87, 105, 116.

With best wishes,


Steve
